passage:
I'm Rashmi, and I still remember the flush in my cheeks when Yash asked for the same report format a third time. My first reaction was defensive. Then I asked, "Can you show me which part isn't meeting the standard?"

Yash pulled up my last two drafts side by side. The headings didn't match, and the summary buried the one number the team needed. I said, "That's on me. I rushed the last one." I made a checklist, sent Yash a draft on Wednesday for a quick look, and the next report went through unchanged.

Looking back, the feedback stung less than vagueness would have. Clear words were a form of respect. They assumed I could do better.

qa.a: Yash pulled up Rashmi's last two drafts side by side.

qa.a: Embarrassed, with a flush in the cheeks, and at first defensive.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that turned feedback into improvement?
qa.a: Rashmi asked for specifics, owned the rushing, made a checklist and sent a draft for a quick look.

qa.q: How might Yash have seen Rashmi's response?
qa.a: Yash probably saw someone who wanted to improve; the account says the clear words assumed Rashmi could do better.

grounding: A junior asked for the same standard again feels embarrassed, asks for specifics, owns the gap and shows improvement without excuses.

passage:
Supervisor's note, analytics team, 12 June.

Today I returned Ankita's market report for the second time. The first version had numbers without sources; this one had sources but no summary a client could use. I kept my comments short and specific.

Ankita's ears went red when I handed it back. For a moment she looked as if she would argue, then said, "Can you show me one report that does this well, so I know exactly what you mean?" I gave her last year's report from Vinita, our senior analyst, and asked Vinita to spend twenty minutes with her.

Ankita did not make excuses. She said, "I rushed the summary. That's on me."

She resubmitted on Friday. The summary was one clear page, with three recommendations and the evidence under each. I told her so, specifically. She let out a breath and smiled for the first time that week.

Next: give her the client presentation in July.

qa.q: What was missing from Ankita's second version of the report?
qa.a: It had sources but no summary a client could use.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when the report came back a second time?
qa.a: Ankita felt embarrassed, her ears going red, and for a moment defensive.

qa.q: What did Ankita do that turned the feedback into improvement?
qa.a: She asked for a specific example, owned the gap without excuses, learned from Vinita and resubmitted a much clearer report.

qa.q: How does the supervisor see clear feedback?
qa.a: The supervisor sees it as respect, keeping comments specific and praising the improvement just as specifically.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a junior asked for the same standard again, who feels embarrassed, asks for specifics, owns the gap and improves without excuses.

passage:
Wednesday, late.

Madhuri sent my brochure design back again. Third time. Her note just said: "Still not the standard. Let's talk tomorrow." I'm the youngest girl in the studio and I felt about twelve years old, sitting there with my face hot.

My first instinct was to explain. The client changed the brief! The printer's template was wrong! All true, a bit. None of it the real problem.

So at the meeting I said, "Can you show me exactly where it falls short?" She did: the spacing was uneven and the headline font fought with the logo. It was so obvious once she pointed.

"I didn't check it at print size," I said. "I'll fix that and check every page before I send."

She nodded. "That's all I wanted."

I redid it by six. She wrote back one word: "Yes." I'm Dolma, and I'm framing that email. Only half joking. 😊

qa.a: It said, "Still not the standard. Let's talk tomorrow."

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when the design came back a third time?
qa.a: Dolma felt embarrassed, face hot, and about twelve years old.

qa.q: Why was asking for specifics better than explaining?
qa.a: Asking exactly where it fell short showed the real gap, so Dolma could own it and fix it, instead of defending with excuses.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Dolma's response at the meeting?
qa.a: Madhuri seems satisfied and respectful, saying "That's all I wanted" once Dolma owned the gap.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young designer asked again for the same standard, who feels embarrassed, asks for specifics, owns the gap and improves without excuses.
